docs.title: Reporting and Measure Execution Model
docs.text:
oa-cohorts defines the core domain model for building reusable cohort logic, compiling it to SQL, and materialising time-stamped qualification events for downstream reporting.

Every executable unit ultimately resolves to a set of MeasureMember rows:

{person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver, measure_date}

That canonical shape lets reports, indicators, and dashboards reuse the same underlying logic while preserving timing and episode alignment.

Diagnosis-related measurements, procedures, and observations with valid explicit episode relationships retain those relationships. An event without a valid recorded link is assigned to one eligible episode of care using the date-window and ranking rules.

For example, suppose a patient's first lung cancer episode starts on 10 January 2024 and remains active during ongoing care through 30 June 2026. A second primary lung cancer episode starts on 1 March 2026, and an unlinked spirometry result is recorded on 10 March 2026. Both episodes are eligible and have already started, so the ranked fallback assigns the result to the second episode because its start is nearest to the measurement date. A valid explicit relationship bypasses this fallback: a relationship to the first episode assigns the result there, while valid relationships to both episodes retain both clinical assertions. The unlinked result is therefore associated with the second cancer, rather than every overlapping episode.

Note that if there has been a change to materialized-view definitions, installing the Python packages does not alter materialized-view definitions already stored in the database. You will need to rebuild any changed materialised views before running reports. Rebuild their dependent views in dependency order and ANALYZE each immediately after creating it. Refreshing a materialized view updates its data but does not replace its definition. See Rebuilding and refreshing clinical materialized views for the schema maintenance guidance.

docs.title: Layer 6: Report
docs.text:
A Report orchestrates cohort and indicator execution for a specific reporting context.

Reports:

  • group together one or more dashboard cohorts
  • execute cohort and indicator measures in a coordinated way
  • treat measure_id = 0 as the special "full report cohort" denominator
  • assemble final output rows with preserved numerator and denominator dates

Reports do not compile measure SQL themselves. They consume MeasureMember results produced lower in the stack.

docs.title: Layer 5: Dash Cohort
docs.text:
A DashCohort defines a clinically meaningful population by grouping one or more cohort definitions, each of which wraps a single measure.

A cohort's members are the union of its underlying definitions. In downstream reporting systems those definitions can be surfaced as sub-cohorts for filtering or drill-down, but their primary role is to create a stable population boundary for indicator logic.

docs.title: Layer 4: Indicator
docs.text:
Indicators compose measures into:

  • denominator: who is in scope
  • numerator: which in-scope members met the target condition

Both numerator and denominator resolve independently to MeasureMember rows. Final report payloads keep both dates:

  • denominator_date
  • numerator_date

Indicator-level relative date windows are applied during payload assembly, not embedded in reusable measure definitions. This keeps measures broad and reusable while allowing different reports to impose different timing rules.

docs.title: Layer 3: Measure
docs.text:
A Measure is a recursive logical node that compiles to SQL and produces MeasureMember rows.

Measures can be:

  • leaf measures backed by a single subquery

  • composite measures backed by child measures

  • Leaf: wraps a single subquery

  • Composite: combination of child measures via OR / AND / EXCEPT
  • Temporal window: event B relative to event A, with configurable bounds and pick strategy (see MeasureTemporalWindow)

Measures are compiled by MeasureSQLCompiler and executed by MeasureExecutor.

docs.title: Layer 2: Subquery
docs.text:
A Subquery is the atomic SQL-producing unit.

It defines:

  • a RuleTarget
  • a RuleTemporality
  • one or more QueryRule objects

Subqueries are responsible for:

  • resolving the measurable class for their target
  • choosing the field that each rule should inspect
  • generating ANY, FIRST, and UNDATED SQL variants

All subqueries emit the canonical measure-member columns:

Column Meaning person_id individual identifier episode_id clinical episode measure_resolver logical alignment key, usually the episode id measure_date date on which the criterion was satisfied

Rule handling inside a subquery:

  • each rule contributes its own WHERE clause fragment
  • rule-level selects are combined with UNION ALL
  • FIRST collapses those candidate rows to the earliest qualifying date per resolver

Value-column resolution depends on the rule types present:

  • exact, hierarchy, presence, and absence rules use a concept-like field
  • substring rules use the measurable's string field
  • predicate rules use the measurable's predicate field
  • scalar rules always use the measurable's numeric field for threshold comparison
  • scalar rules only require a concept field when at least one scalar rule has concept_id != 0

That last point is important for derived window measurables such as tx_to_death_window and referral_to_specialist_window: threshold-only scalar rules can run against numeric-only measurables.

RuleTarget selection also carries clinical meaning, not just technical routing. For example:

  • dx_any resolves against any diagnosis row attached to the current episode
  • dx_primary resolves against diagnosis rows anchored to the patient's primary diagnosis episode

That distinction lets report authors choose whether a cohort should follow episode-level diagnosis coding broadly, or whether it should stay anchored to the diagnosis present at the start of the primary episode of care.

docs.title: Layer 1: QueryRule
docs.text:
A QueryRule is the smallest declarative unit in the engine: a single predicate applied to a field resolved by a subquery.

Examples:

  • diagnosis concept equals X
  • numeric value is less than Y
  • predicate column is true
  • concept code contains substring Z

A rule does not generate a standalone query. It only contributes a WHERE clause fragment within a subquery.

docs.title: Why MeasureMember Rows Matter
docs.text:
The engine preserves qualification rows instead of reducing everything to a single boolean membership flag.

That supports:

  • trend analysis over time
  • indicator windows anchored to cohort membership dates
  • episode-aware joins for AND logic
  • multiple qualifying events per person when OR logic applies

This is the core design choice that makes the reporting layer flexible without forcing each report to redefine its own SQL.

docs.title: Episode attachment and measure resolution
docs.text: This page explains which cancer an assessment or treatment belongs to, and how that affects its quality indicators. It starts with the clinical rules and examples, then gives the details needed to use the data in queries. For how several records become one indicator result, see From clinical evidence to one indicator result.

docs.title: Which cancers enter the report?
docs.text:
The cohort identifies a patient’s cancer by its diagnosis: one episode of care per top-level MOSAIQ diagnosis. A diagnosis recorded under another diagnosis is a nested diagnosis. It belongs to the same cancer and does not create a separate cohort entry when the cohort selects primary diagnoses, as described below. An indicator can then count cancers individually or count each patient once.

Treatment careplans and performed surgery reach the diagnosis recorded in the source. Care on a nested progression or metastatic diagnosis also counts for its same-patient episode of care, while remaining available on the nested diagnosis. This follows the recorded parent and does not move care between primaries.

Measurements, assessments, procedures and observations use valid recorded episode links when available; otherwise they use the date-window rules below. Specialist visits have a separate attachment rule.

Assumption: cohorts select through the primary diagnosis

Every leaf measure reachable from a cohort definition must select through the primary diagnosis (dx_primary). Under this assumption, each cohort row identifies an episode of care. A nested diagnosis is not a cohort row even when its diagnosis codes match the cohort definition.

Cohorts defined through any diagnosis (dx_any), stage (dx_stage) or metastasis (dx_mets) can also select nested diagnoses. The one-entry-per-cancer interpretation on this page does not apply to those definitions.

Two top-level diagnoses for one patient are treated as true second primaries, so the patient can have two cohort rows. Duplicate entry of one cancer as two top-level diagnoses is assumed to be managed through clinical data review; these rules do not merge those diagnoses.

docs.title: Attachment rules
docs.text: Area Behaviour Recorded event links Keep every link that matches the event, its type, the episode and the patient; suppress date-window fallback for that event Date-window attachment Choose one eligible episode of care; nested diagnoses are not fallback candidates Window From 90 days before the episode starts to its recorded end date, or start + 365 days when no end is recorded; extend its end to the latest nested-diagnosis window end when that is later Nested-diagnosis treatment Keep direct evidence and credit its valid episode-of-care parent; deduplicate performed source activity Measure criteria Combine evidence for the same patient and cancer; apply exclusions to that cancer Indicator evaluation Check the criteria and date windows for each cancer; count each patient once if the indicator is configured to count patients

docs.title: Step 1: how a clinical event finds an episode
docs.text:
1. Recorded links. Validate each recorded relationship against the event ID, kind of event, episode and patient. Keep every valid relationship, including relationships to nested diagnoses and relationships outside the date window. An event can retain several valid links. It does not also enter date-window fallback.
  2. Date window. For an event without a valid recorded link, consider the patient's episodes of care whose windows contain the event date. Each window starts 90 days before the episode starts and closes at the later of its own window end and the latest window end of its nested diagnoses. Each episode's window ends on its recorded end date, or 365 days after its start when no end is recorded. A later progression or metastasis therefore extends eligibility for the same cancer. The original cancer’s window still starts at the same date.
  3. Choosing one. Prefer candidates that had already started on the event date, then choose the most recent start. If none had started, choose the nearest upcoming start. If start dates are equal, choose the lower episode number. When the nearest eligible already-started episode began at least 365 days before the event, choose the earliest eligible upcoming episode starting within 60 days after the event, breaking equal starts by the lowest episode ID. Both thresholds are inclusive. A more recent started episode blocks this override, and a same-day start is already started. No concept list is used.
  4. No candidate. The event has no diagnosis-episode attachment through this route, so an indicator using these diagnosis-linked event views cannot use it.
flowchart TD event["Clinical event"] --> linked{"Any recorded link matchingthe event type, episode and patient?"} linked -- "Yes" --> recorded["Keep every valid recorded relationship(may include nested diagnoses)and stop"] linked -- "No" --> window["Candidates: the patient's episodes of carewhose windows contain the event date"] window --> eligible{"Any eligible candidate?"} eligible -- "No" --> none["No diagnosis-episode attachment"] eligible -- "Yes" --> started{"Any candidate already startedon the event date?"} started -- "Yes" --> recent["Keep those already started;choose the most recent start"] started -- "No" --> nearest["Choose the nearest upcoming start"] recent --> override{"Started winner at least 365 days oldand upcoming start within 60 days?"} override -- "Yes" --> upcoming["Choose the earliest eligible upcoming start"] override -- "No" --> tie upcoming --> tie["Equal start dates:lower episode number"] nearest --> tie tie --> one["Attach to one episode of care"]

Specialist visits use a separate assignment based on proximity to the episode start. They do not use the event ranking above and may appear against more than one episode.

docs.title: Step 2: how the report checks an indicator
docs.text:
1. Cohort. Create one cohort row per episode of care that meets the cohort definition, dated at diagnosis. This depends on the primary-diagnosis assumption above.
  2. Criteria inside a measure. Inclusions select records and exclusions remove them. OR accepts evidence for either criterion. AND requires both criteria for the same cancer. EXCEPT keeps cancers meeting its first criterion only when they do not meet the other criteria. The measure retains the dates needed to check timing later.
  3. Denominator and numerator. The denominator identifies eligible cancers, either the whole cohort or a subset meeting specified criteria. The numerator identifies which of those cancers meet the indicator. In both cases, the evidence must belong to the same cancer and satisfy the configured date windows.
  4. Counting patients. If the indicator counts patients rather than cancers, check each cancer first. Then count the patient once in the denominator if any cancer is eligible, and once in the numerator if any eligible cancer meets the criterion. Keep the supporting evidence from the cancer that meets it.

Evidence for one primary cannot satisfy an indicator for another, and repeated records do not cause the same cancer to be counted again. If a date needed to establish eligibility is missing, show the result as unresolved and exclude it from both totals. Numerator evidence also needs a date unless the question explicitly accepts undated records and has no date window. The worked resolution examples explain these cases and how results are assigned to reporting periods.

docs.title: Worked example 1: one cancer with a later nested diagnosis
docs.text:
• E1 is a lung episode of care diagnosed 10 March 2025, with no recorded end date. Its own window runs from 10 December 2024 to 10 March 2026. P1 extends its upper bound to 1 September 2026.
  • P1 is brain metastases recorded beneath the lung diagnosis from 1 September 2025, with no recorded end date. Its own window ends on 1 September 2026. It can receive valid recorded links but is not a date-window candidate.
Event Attachment Reason GP referral, 20 Feb 2025 E1 Its date is inside E1's window ECOG A, 25 Mar 2025 E1 Its date is inside E1's window Chemotherapy careplan recorded against the brain-metastases diagnosis P1 and E1 The nested diagnosis retains its evidence and its root also receives credit ECOG B, 15 Oct 2025 E1 P1 is not a date-window candidate ECOG C, 20 Apr 2026 E1 P1 extends E1's window through 1 September 2026

For the E1 cohort row:

Indicator Kind Result under the stated rules ECOG documented Whole cohort Met: ECOG A is on E1 Received systemic therapy Whole cohort Treatment is available on E1; it qualifies only if the treatment date meets the indicator window Stage III NSCLC with ECOG 0–2 Defined denominator Met if stage III is on E1 and its ECOG evidence meets the criterion and date window Stage III NSCLC who received systemic therapy Defined denominator Treatment on P1 counts for E1 when stage and treatment meet the indicator criteria and window

Chemotherapy beginning 20 September is more than 90 days after E1's diagnosis. Root attribution makes the treatment available on E1, but it does not qualify for a 0..90-day indicator. A performed surgery on P1 likewise removes E1's false no-surgery state; a historical-surgery observation alone does not.

ECOG C occurs after E1's own 365-day horizon but inside the extended window. It reaches E1 through date-window fallback. P1 contributes its window end, but its start never competes with another primary's start in the ranking. If E1's own end already covers P1, extension does not shorten it.

docs.title: Worked example 2: two lung primaries
docs.text:
• E1 is the first lung primary, diagnosed 1 June 2025, with a recorded end of 30 June 2026. Its window runs from 3 March 2025 to 30 June 2026.
  • E2 is the second lung primary, diagnosed 1 March 2026, with no recorded end date. Its window runs from 1 December 2025 to 1 March 2027.
Event Attachment under the stated rules Why GP referral 1, 10 May 2025 E1 Only E1's window contains it GP referral 2 for the new lesion, 5 Feb 2026 E1 Both windows contain it, but E1 is less than 365 days old, so the upcoming-episode preference does not apply Spirometry, 10 Mar 2026 E2 Both had started; E2 has the more recent start MDT presentation, 12 Mar 2026 E2 As for spirometry

The spirometry and MDT attach once, to E2. The referral for the new lesion attaches to E1 under the already-started preference, so it cannot start an E2 referral-to-specialist or referral-to-treatment calculation through episode-aligned matching. The upcoming-episode preference does not apply because E1 is less than 365 days old at the referral. If E1 instead began on 1 June 2024 and remained eligible, that 5 February referral would attach to E2: E1 is then at least 365 days old and E2 begins within 60 days. A valid explicit link to E1 still takes precedence.

Ranking by dates alone does not establish which cancer an event concerns. If E2 were a prostate primary, the lung MDT would still attach to E2 under this rule. Attachment is independent of the kind or content of an event.

docs.title: Episode links supplied by omop-constructs
docs.text:
Evidence Identity and attribution Generic events Source table, source event ID and attached episode ID; valid explicit links take precedence over date-based assignment Treatment and performed surgery Recorded disease owner plus its eligible episode-of-care root; physical activity is deduplicated per target Treatment intent Source measurement IDs distinguish different records even when their concepts and dates agree Treatment summaries Wide regimen × course combinations and condition-date envelope rows; raw row counts are not patient or treatment counts

The existing treatment measurables consume the attributed condition episode IDs. Indicator criteria and diagnosis-time evidence windows determine whether that attributed evidence qualifies for a report.

View-definition changes require a rebuild, followed by immediate ANALYZE in dependency order. See Rebuilding and refreshing clinical materialized views.

docs.title: Matching and counting in oa-cohorts
docs.text:
Measures retain person, episode, resolver and evidence dates. Both whole-cohort and defined-denominator indicators match (person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver) before applying date windows. Missing episode linkage does not match. They produce one result per cancer; the configuration field grain=patient combines those cancer results into one result per patient. The default, grain=episode, counts cancers separately. Patient output rows use person_id as their resolver and include the cancer identities that support the result.

Treatment attribution and indicator timing are separate operations. An episode window determines which cancer can receive otherwise unlinked evidence; it does not replace a diagnosis-relative criterion or an interval between two events.

For configuring a window between diagnosis and another event, see Temporal windows.

docs.title: From clinical evidence to one indicator result
docs.text:
A patient may have several assessments and treatments for the same cancer. Each record can help establish whether an indicator is met, but it should not cause that cancer to be counted again. Measures collect and combine this evidence. Indicators use it to decide which cancers are eligible (the denominator), which meet the criterion (the numerator), and whether the report counts cancers or patients.

The counts are numerator / denominator. Several records for A produce one cancer result. When counting patients, P1 meets the indicator through A; B is still not shown as having received RT.

Episode attachment is a separate decision from timing. A measurement attached to cancer B cannot pass an indicator for cancer A merely because the same patient has both. Episode attachment explains recorded links, fallback date windows and nested diagnoses.

docs.title: Several records, one result
docs.text:
The following fictional patient has two lung primaries. The event labels distinguish the records; two events can remain separate even when they share a date. RT means radiotherapy.

Patient Cancer Event Date Evidence P1 Lung A E1 10 Jan 2026 Stage III P1 Lung A E2 20 Jan 2026 RT start P1 Lung A E3 15 Feb 2026 Further RT start P1 Lung B E4 1 Apr 2026 Stage III

For Stage III AND RT, A qualifies and B does not. For Stage III OR RT, both qualify. Several records for A still count as one eligible cancer.

Expression Evidence retained First date A meets the criteria Stage III OR RT E1, E2 and E3 10 Jan Stage III AND RT Supporting stage and RT records, with completion dates 20 Jan Stage III EXCEPT RT A is excluded because it has RT; B remains None for A

For an AND, the first qualifying date is the later of the earliest qualifying dates for its two criteria: MAX(earliest qualifying A, earliest qualifying B). In this example, stage was recorded on 10 January and RT began on 20 January, so both requirements had been met by 20 January. This does not establish that the stage assessment was still clinically current when RT began. If that matters to the question, the definition needs a date window.

docs.title: Check the date window before choosing an assessment
docs.text:
Suppose diagnosis is 1 March, eligible RT starts 20 March, and assessment must be within 10 days before RT through RT start, inclusive.

Assessment date Difference from RT Qualifies? 1 March −19 days No 10 March −10 days Yes, lower boundary 15 March −5 days Yes 20 March 0 days Yes, upper boundary 21 March +1 day No

The assessment on 1 March is too early, but it must not hide the valid assessment on 15 March. First find assessments inside the window, then apply the choice specified by the measure: keep all, the earliest, the latest, or the closest to treatment. In configuration these are any, earliest, latest and closest. Equally close assessments are ordered by earlier date, then source identifier. The 10-day interval is illustrative; each indicator needs its own clinical definition.

These three dates answer different questions. The configuration calls the event being checked the candidate and the event it is compared with the anchor:

Date role This example Meaning Assessment (candidate) 15 March When assessment happened Treatment (anchor) 20 March The date the assessment is compared with Completion 20 March When both dated requirements had occurred

The measure can return the assessment date, the treatment date, or the earlier or later of the two. Its completion date is stored separately. For a later question about treatment start or end, use that treatment date rather than the date when a combined set of criteria was first met.

docs.title: A question about first treatment must use the first treatment
docs.text:
Eligible treatment Start Assessment in its preceding 10 days First-treatment question Any-treatment question T1 20 March None Fails No qualifying assessment T2 19 April 14 April Cannot rescue T1 Passes through T2

Both questions count one eligible cancer. The first-treatment question fails because T1 has no qualifying assessment; the any-treatment question passes because T2 does. To answer the first-treatment question, select T1 before checking whether an assessment meets the criterion.

Start and end must belong to the same selected treatment. If T1 starts 10 January and ends 2 March, while T2 starts 20 January and ends 10 February, “end of the first treatment” is 2 March. It is not the earliest end among all treatments. The configuration therefore separates how a treatment is selected from which of its dates is used for comparison.

To count curative RT, the RT and curative intent must belong to the same recorded treatment. Palliative RT plus curative systemic anticancer therapy (SACT) does not establish curative RT. Repeated records of the same intent are retained. If one treatment has conflicting recorded intents, it is excluded from intent-specific criteria because its intent is uncertain. The treatment-intent data used here cannot identify cycles with no recorded intent; missing intent needs to be checked in the source data.

docs.title: Does the window run from diagnosis or treatment?
docs.text:
Question Denominator Numerator timing Result for the example Documented assessment Eligible cancer No window Met if a dated assessment is recorded Assessment within 30 days of diagnosis Cancer diagnosed 1 March Relative to 1 March 15 March passes Assessment before first eligible RT First eligible RT on 20 March Relative to selected RT 15 March passes in the example’s 10 days before RT

By default, indicator windows run from the cohort date, usually diagnosis. Selecting treated cancers as the denominator does not change that reference date. To compare an assessment with the eligible treatment instead, set numerator_reference=denominator. Use a temporal-window measure for questions about specific start/end dates or more than one timing relationship.

When comparing with a treatment, evidence recorded against a particular treatment must refer to the selected treatment. An assessment with no treatment ID is checked by its date, within the same cancer.

docs.title: Should the indicator count cancers or patients?
docs.text:
The configuration field grain controls this choice: episode counts each eligible cancer, while patient counts each eligible patient once. The default is episode.

Patient Cancer Eligible? Criterion met? P1 A Yes No P1 B Yes Yes P2 C Yes No Count Denominator Numerator Interpretation Cancers 3 1 One of three eligible cancers meets the criterion Patients 2 1 One of two eligible patients has a cancer that meets the criterion

When counting patients, first check each cancer separately. A patient is eligible if any of their cancers is eligible, and meets the indicator if any eligible cancer meets its criterion. Here P1 meets the indicator through cancer B. The result keeps B’s supporting evidence so the reader can see why. An earlier date from cancer A may determine P1’s reporting period, but it must not be shown as the treatment date that justified the result for B.

Repeated dates and cohort labels for one cancer do not increase the count. An indicator whose denominator is the whole cohort uses each cancer’s earliest dated cohort reference. Evidence for one primary cannot satisfy the criterion for another.

docs.title: Missing information and reporting periods
docs.text:
“No surgery recorded” does not have a surgery date. When an absence rule is combined with dated criteria, it checks eligibility without supplying a date: stage recorded on 10 January AND no surgery recorded qualifies on 10 January. Its source date stays empty. This differs from surgery that is recorded but has no usable date; that missing date cannot establish when a dated requirement was met. An absence-only measure cannot supply the anchor or candidate date for a window.

Death criteria check for an OMOP death record, independently of gender or other demographics. They use the calendar date of death_datetime, falling back to death_date when there is no timestamp. No death record means the death criterion is not met; it does not mean the patient is known to be alive. A recorded death with neither date available remains unresolved when its date is required.

If a date needed to establish eligibility is missing, the result is unresolved. Show it separately and exclude it from both numerator and denominator totals (denominator_value=false). If the cancer is eligible but has no qualifying numerator evidence, the criterion has not been demonstrated; that does not prove care was omitted. Undated numerator evidence is excluded by default. The presence setting can accept it when a question only asks whether something was recorded, but it cannot establish that an event fell within a date window.

Evidence Eligibility Contribution Dated eligible denominator, passing numerator Eligible Denominator 1, numerator 1 Dated eligible denominator, no qualifying numerator Eligible Denominator 1, numerator 0 Required denominator date missing Unresolved Neither total; show unresolved count No denominator membership Outside the eligible set Neither total

The indicator’s period_date determines where its result appears in a monthly or yearly report. It can come from the cohort, denominator, numerator or completion date. For example, if two AND criteria are met on 31 January and 1 February, their completion date is 1 February. A report using completion dates counts that result once, in February. Use the same period date for both numerator and denominator totals, and show results with missing period dates as unassigned rather than guessing a date.

When counting patients, cohort or denominator dates use the earliest eligible reference across their cancers. Numerator or completion dates follow the cancer that provides the supporting evidence for the patient’s result.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
These settings make the choices above explicit. The defaults count cancers, accept any eligible treatment opportunity and compare indicator windows with the cohort date. Schema management explains how to upgrade the configuration database.

Location Field Default / options Indicator grain episode counts cancers; patient counts patients Measure matching_scope cancer; treatment additionally requires equal non-null treatment identity Temporal window anchor_selection first; also latest, all Temporal window anchor_order_date_role measure; also start, end, completion Temporal window anchor_date_role, candidate_date_role measure; also start, end, completion Indicator opportunity_selection any; also first Indicator numerator_reference cohort; also denominator Indicator period_date_source denominator; also cohort, numerator, completion Indicator undated_numerator_policy exclude; also presence

When importing a CSV, omitted policy columns leave existing settings unchanged. Blank or unknown values are rejected. For SQL interfaces and the evidence fields available to developers, see Measure resolution.

docs.title: Example Execution
docs.text: This page sketches the current execution flow at a high level. It is intentionally lightweight and reflects the public objects that are exercised in the codebase today.

docs.title: 1. Import configuration
docs.text:
The engine expects reports, cohorts, measures, subqueries, and rules to exist in the database. In this repo that is typically loaded from the CSV files under dash_config/.

Typical CLI flow:

oa-cohorts import-config dash_config

docs.title: 2. Load a report
docs.text:
Once configuration is loaded, a report can be fetched through the ORM and executed against a SQLAlchemy session.

from sqlalchemy import select

from oa_cohorts.query.measure import MeasureExecutor
from oa_cohorts.query.report import Report

report = session.execute(
    select(Report).where(Report.report_short_name == "YOUR_REPORT")
).scalars().unique().one()

executor = MeasureExecutor(session)
report.execute(executor)
report.assert_executed()

docs.title: 3. Access resolved cohort members
docs.text:
After execution, report cohort membership is available as MeasureMember rows.

members = report.members(executor)

Each member preserves:

  • person_id
  • episode_id
  • measure_resolver
  • measure_date

docs.title: 4. Build indicator output
docs.text:
Indicators resolve numerator and denominator measures independently, then join them back to the report cohort during output assembly.

In the current codebase this is handled by the reporting/output layer rather than by the indicator object itself emitting a final flat table.

docs.title: 5. Inspect SQL and structure
docs.text:
Most query objects are also HTMLRenderable, which makes notebook debugging practical:

report
measure
subquery
query_rule

These renderers expose:

  • structural metadata
  • SQL previews where compilation succeeds
  • executability status and failure messages where it does not

docs.title: Notes on current usage
docs.text:
• Measures in the shipped dashboard config are primarily composed with OR and AND.
  • Threshold-only scalar rules use concept_id = 0 and can target numeric-only measurables.
  • Indicator-level relative date windows are applied during payload assembly, anchored to report cohort membership dates.

docs.title: Measurable Abstraction
docs.text:
The Measurable layer is the bridge between the generic query engine and the underlying ORM or materialised-view schema.

It tells the engine:

  • which ORM class to query for a given RuleTarget
  • which columns identify the person, episode, and event date
  • which optional columns support concept, numeric, string, or predicate-style filtering

The query engine never hard-codes source-table column names directly. It relies on the measurable contract instead.

docs.title: Canonical Output Contract
docs.text:
Every measurable must be able to emit rows in the canonical measure-member shape:

Column Meaning person_id individual identifier episode_id clinical episode measure_resolver alignment key used for higher-level joins measure_date date on which the measurable event qualifies

MeasurableBase.table_selectables() and filter_table_dated() produce this shape for subqueries and measures.

docs.title: MeasurableSpec
docs.text:
MeasurableSpec is the declarative mapping attached to each measurable class.

Required attributes:

  • domain
  • label
  • person_id_attr
  • episode_id_attr
  • event_date_attr

Optional value attributes:

  • value_concept_attr
  • value_numeric_attr
  • value_string_attr
  • value_predicate_attr

Optional control fields:

  • temporality_map
  • valid_targets

The spec stores attribute names, not SQLAlchemy columns. Those names are resolved against the concrete class at bind time.

docs.title: Binding
docs.text:
When a class subclasses MeasurableBase and defines:

__measurable__ = MeasurableSpec(...)

the class is automatically bound to a BoundMeasurableSpec via __init_subclass__.

Binding rules:

  • required columns are resolved immediately
  • unsupported optional value channels remain None
  • no fake SQL constants are injected for missing value channels

That last point is intentional. A measurable that does not support concept filtering should expose value_concept_col = None, and the query layer should decide whether that is acceptable for the rules being executed.

docs.title: Which Rule Types Need Which Columns
docs.text:
The current query engine resolves measurable fields like this:

Rule style Required measurable column exact / hierarchy / hierarchy exclusion / presence / absence value_concept_attr substring value_string_attr predicate value_predicate_attr scalar threshold value_numeric_attr scalar threshold with concept_id != 0 value_numeric_attr and value_concept_attr

docs.title: Scalar-only measurables
docs.text:
Derived window measurables can legitimately expose only a numeric column.

Examples in the current codebase:

  • ReferralToSpecialistWindowMeasurable
  • window-style derived thresholds generally driven by ScalarRule

These measurables work when the scalar rule is threshold-only, meaning concept_id = 0.

They do not support concept-constrained scalar filtering. If a scalar rule with concept_id != 0 targets such a measurable, subquery compilation raises a targeted error explaining that value_concept_attr is required for concept filtering.

docs.title: Episode Requirement
docs.text:
This project assumes an episode-linked oncology data model.

Why that matters:

  • a person can have multiple disease episodes
  • diagnosis, treatment, and modifier rows must align to the correct episode
  • composite AND logic joins on measure_resolver, which is usually the episode id

Without an episode-level resolver:

  • AND logic would collapse to person-level intersection
  • cross-episode contamination would become possible
  • time-based qualification would be harder to interpret clinically

docs.title: Current Measurable Families
docs.text:
The shipped registry currently maps targets into a small set of measurable families:

  • diagnosis measurables: any-diagnosis, primary-diagnosis, staging, metastasis
  • event measurables: measurements, procedures, observations
  • treatment measurables: surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, intent, derived windows
  • person measurables: death-linked person demography rows

docs.title: Current Target Registry
docs.text:
The authoritative supported set is the measurable registry, not the RuleTarget enum by itself. Some enum members are reserved for future design work and do not currently resolve to a shipped measurable.

Current registry:

Target Measurable Intended use dx_any AnyConditionMeasurable any diagnosis row attached to an episode dx_primary PrimaryDiagnosisEpisodeMeasurable diagnosis rows anchored to the primary diagnosis episode dx_stage StagedConditionMeasurable staging modifiers linked to diagnosis episodes dx_mets MetsConditionMeasurable metastatic disease modifiers linked to diagnosis episodes tx_surgical SurgicalMeasurable cancer-related surgical procedures tx_current_episode AllCurrentTreatmentMeasurable treatment-start summary for the current diagnosis episode tx_chemotherapy ChemoTreatmentMeasurable chemotherapy treatment episodes tx_radiotherapy RTTreatmentMeasurable radiotherapy treatment episodes intent_sact IntentChemoMeasurable systemic therapy intent flags intent_rt IntentRTMeasurable radiotherapy intent flags tx_to_death_window TxDaysBeforeDeath derived days from treatment to death dx_to_tx_window TxDaysToStartTreatment derived days from diagnosis to treatment start tx_concurrent TxConcurrentChemoRT concurrent chemo-radiotherapy predicate referral_to_specialist_window ReferralToSpecialistWindowMeasurable derived referral-to-specialist interval meas_concept MeasurementMeasurable diagnosis-linked measurements proc_concept ProcedureMeasurable diagnosis-linked procedures obs_concept ObserveMeasurable diagnosis-linked observations ev_visit VisitSpecialtyMeasurable diagnosis-linked specialty visits demog_death DeathMeasurable death-linked person rows

docs.title: Diagnosis Targets
docs.text:
For clinical users, the most important distinction is between the two diagnosis concept targets:

  • dx_any asks whether a diagnosis row is present on the episode being evaluated
  • dx_primary asks whether the diagnosis belongs to the patient's primary diagnosis episode anchor

dx_primary is intended for cohort definitions that should be stable at the start of the primary episode of care, rather than changing because later progression or metastatic episodes carry related diagnosis coding.

That design is deliberate. It lets the same reporting engine support both:

  • broad episode-level diagnosis logic
  • primary-diagnosis anchored cohort logic

without forcing report authors to invent bespoke SQL or special-case post-processing.

docs.title: String-backed Filters
docs.text:
SubstringRule works against the measurable's value_string_attr, but those string fields are not all the same kind of data.

Current examples include:

  • diagnosis code strings such as condition_code
  • derived labels such as stage_label
  • event labels such as event_label
  • treatment names such as surgery_name, regimen_concept, and course_concept
  • provider specialty labels such as provider_specialty

That is why the measurable contract matters: the rule engine only knows that it is applying a substring filter to the target's declared string field.

See src/oa_cohorts/measurables/measurable_resolver.py for the authoritative target-to-class registry.

docs.title: Measure Resolution
docs.text: For worked clinical examples, counting rules and date roles, start with From clinical evidence to one indicator result. This page describes the SQL projections.

docs.title: The evidence returned by a measure
docs.text:
A measure returns MeasureMember rows. These identify the patient, cancer and date; additional fields retain source identifiers, treatment identifiers and dates needed by later criteria. The four core fields are:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MeasureMember:
    person_id: int
    measure_resolver: int
    episode_id: Optional[int]
    measure_date: Optional[date]

A MeasureMember is not just a boolean membership flag. It captures:

  • which patient and cancer the evidence belongs to
  • which episode is used for matching (measure_resolver)
  • the date returned by the measure

This preserved timing is what allows indicator windows, per-period reporting, and episode-aware logic to work later in the pipeline.

docs.title: Combining criteria
docs.text: Measures combine evidence using OR, AND and EXCEPT. They retain the records and dates needed by later criteria. The indicator decides how that evidence contributes to the final count.

docs.title: OR: preserve all qualifying rows
docs.text:
OR keeps distinct qualifying evidence, deduplicating the same physical event.

Implementation shape:

  • each child supplies evidence rows
  • rows are combined with UNION
  • all qualifying dates are preserved

Example:

  • measure = ECOG 0 OR ECOG 1

If the same person qualifies on two different dates, both rows survive.

This is the full evidence result. The four-column sql_any() projection can merge distinct events that share a cancer and date; sql_evidence() retains their source identities.

docs.title: AND: both criteria for the same cancer
docs.text:
AND requires all child criteria to be met for the same cancer. Matching only the patient would allow evidence from one primary to qualify another.

Implementation shape:

  • child rows are aligned by (person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver)
  • first qualification is the latest of the earliest child completions; branch evidence remains available
  • rows with mismatched resolvers do not qualify together

This gives the first date by which all required events had occurred. If the criteria must be met close together in time, add an explicit date window.

Example:

  • measure = Stage III AND Radiotherapy

If Stage III qualifies under episode 10 and Radiotherapy qualifies under episode 10, the composite measure qualifies.

If the two child rows belong to different episodes, they do not intersect.

The stage record keeps its original source_date of 10 January. Its combined measure_date and completion_date are 20 January, when both requirements had occurred. Later RT evidence also remains available. sql_qualification() returns the first completion date for the cancer.

docs.title: Choosing a SQL result
docs.text:
Use the query that answers the question being asked:

  • sql_evidence() preserves qualifying records, source identities and date roles.
  • sql_any() returns distinct rows with the four core fields.
  • sql_first() returns the earliest emitted date per (person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver).
  • sql_qualification() returns the earliest completion date per cancer: when all dated requirements had occurred.
  • sql_undated() returns distinct membership keys without dates; it is unsupported for temporal-window measures.

MeasureExecutor retains the evidence fields and scopes its cache to the selected people and episode override. Cumulative AND combines each child’s evidence with the other children’s earliest completions, so 32 records from each of two children need at most 64 evidence rows rather than 1,024 pairs.

docs.title: Temporal Window: Event-to-Event Timing
docs.text:
A third measure kind handles cases where qualification depends on the relationship between two events — specifically, whether event B occurs within a defined window relative to event A.

This is expressed via MeasureTemporalWindow, a separate config table with a 1:1 relationship to Measure (enforced by primary key). A measure with a window_config row is a temporal window measure.

Anchor and candidate

The anchor uses exactly one source: the measure's subquery_id, or MeasureTemporalWindow.anchor_measure_id pointing to another dated measure. A separate candidate_measure_id identifies the events evaluated relative to that anchor. A measure anchor runs its own filters first; only then does its declared first/latest/all anchor selection run per (person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver). The default anchor selection is first. Missing references, two anchor sources, reversed bounds and dependency cycles are rejected before SQL compilation.

Window bounds

window_min_days and window_max_days are optional. NULL means unbounded on that side. Negative values are valid — a candidate event occurring before the anchor can still qualify when it falls within the configured bounds. The selected result date is returned as measure_date; the supporting event dates remain available in the evidence fields.

Pick strategy (window_pick_strategy)

Controls which candidate events are retained for each selected anchor, after applying the window filter:

Value Behaviour any All qualifying candidate events are preserved earliest Earliest qualifying candidate for each selected anchor latest Latest qualifying candidate for each selected anchor closest Qualifying candidate closest to each selected anchor

Default when NULL: earliest.

Result date (result_date_source)

Controls which date is emitted as measure_date in the output:

Value Emitted date candidate Date of the candidate event anchor Date of the anchor event greatest Later of anchor or candidate least Earlier of anchor or candidate

Default when NULL: candidate.

Resolver alignment (require_same_resolver)

When TRUE (default), the anchor and candidate must match on (person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver). When FALSE, matching uses person_id only. Reserve that setting for intentionally patient-level facts; it permits matching across the patient’s cancers.

SQL variants

sql_any() and sql_first() are supported. sql_undated() raises NotImplementedError — this surfaces as WARN (not FAIL) in is_executable() because the measure is still usable in the normal execution path.

Configuration

Temporal window measures are loaded via measure_temporal_window.csv in the config directory. The CSV is optional — existing deployments without it are unaffected.

Example — GP referral to treatment within 42 days:

Measure:
  name:        GP referral to first treatment or pall care <= 42d
  combination: rule_or
  subquery_id: <GP referral subquery>

MeasureTemporalWindow:
  candidate_measure_id: <any treatment OR pall care composite>
  window_min_days:      NULL
  window_max_days:      42
  window_pick_strategy: earliest
  result_date_source:   candidate
  require_same_resolver: TRUE

docs.title: Nested Measures
docs.text:
Measures can be nested arbitrarily:

A AND (B OR C)

Evaluation proceeds bottom-up:

  1. B OR C resolves to all qualifying child rows
  2. A resolves independently
  3. AND matches evidence on (person_id, episode_id, measure_resolver)
  4. its first qualification is the later of A’s and the qualifying alternative’s earliest completion dates

The supporting evidence remains available to later measures and indicator windows.

docs.title: Atomic Rule Types (QueryRule)
docs.text:
QueryRule is the smallest declarative unit in the engine.

Each rule:

  • targets a field resolved by a Subquery
  • produces a SQL WHERE clause fragment
  • participates in rule-level UNION ALL composition inside the subquery

Choose a rule according to the field you want to test: a code, a number, a boolean flag or a string. The measurable supplies that field and determines which records are available to test. A rule filters those records; it does not decide which cancer an event belongs to or how many cancers or patients the indicator counts.

The examples below use invented concept IDs and records. Assume the example concepts and their stated relationships are present in the vocabulary; they are not clinical concept mappings to copy into a report. NULL means a missing value.

docs.title: Combining rules: either is different from both
docs.text:
During measure execution, multiple rules in one subquery are alternatives. Each rule selects records, and the results are combined with UNION ALL. For example, two exact rules for ECOG 0 and ECOG 1 mean “ECOG 0 or ECOG 1”, not “both”.

Record Recorded ECOG Exact rule for ECOG 0 Exact rule for ECOG 1 Selected by the subquery? M1 0 Yes No Yes M2 1 No Yes Yes M3 2 No No No

Here 0, 1 and 2 are the clinical score labels; the exact rules use the corresponding vocabulary concept IDs. If the source instead stores a numeric score, use a scalar rule against that numeric field.

To require stage III and radiotherapy, put those criteria in separate measures and combine them with AND. The criteria must match the same cancer. If the question concerns curative RT, modality and intent must also refer to the same treatment; combining arbitrary records from the same patient or cancer would not establish that. See Combining criteria and treatment identity.

For developers calling SQL helpers directly: compiled measure execution uses get_subquery_evidence(), which combines rule alternatives. The lower-level Subquery.select() and where_clause() helpers combine rule predicates with AND; they are not an equivalent preview of a multi-rule measure.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Match rows whose concept-like field equals a single OMOP concept id.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field = concept_id

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Precise coded events such as a single diagnosis, procedure, or referral concept.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
An exact rule with concept_id=1100 keeps only records coded 1100. It does not include related concepts automatically.

Recorded concept Selected? Why 1100 Yes Exact match 1000, the parent of 1100 No Related, but a different concept 1200, another concept in the same family No Related, but a different concept NULL No No value to match

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Expand one OMOP concept into its descendants using concept_ancestor, then match any descendant concept.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field IN (descendant_concept_ids)

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Broad diagnosis or procedure groupings such as stage families or disease branches.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Suppose the hierarchy rows for ancestor 1000 include 1000 itself and descendants 1100 and 1200. A hierarchy rule for 1000 accepts all three.

Recorded concept Selected? Why 1000 Yes The hierarchy contains the self-relationship 1000 → 1000 1100 Yes Descendant of 1000 1200 Yes Descendant of 1000 2000 No Outside that hierarchy NULL No No value to match

The rule reads concept_ancestor; it does not infer relationships from concept names or code prefixes. Parent matching depends on the self-relationship being present.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Exclude a concept and all of its descendants.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field NOT IN (descendant_concept_ids)

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Filtering individual records outside an unwanted concept family.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Using the same family {1000, 1100, 1200}, a hierarchy exclusion rule for 1000 selects records outside that set.

Recorded concept Selected? 1000 No 1100 No 2000 Yes NULL No: SQL NOT IN does not treat a null as a known value outside the set

This filters records, not every record belonging to a cancer. If one cancer has records coded both 1100 and 2000, its 2000 record can still pass this rule. To exclude the cancer whenever it has evidence in the unwanted family, use a measure-level EXCEPT with that family as the exclusion criterion. A hierarchy exclusion alone also does not supply a positive definition such as “lung cancer”.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Match rows where the resolved field is non-null.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field IS NOT NULL

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Checking whether the field supplied by the chosen measurable has a value.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
For a concept-like field, presence means non-null; it does not mean “known, valid clinical code”.

Field in an available row PresenceRule selects it? 1100 Yes 0 Yes: zero is a value, not SQL NULL NULL No No row supplied by the measurable No row exists for the rule to select

The target determines what is being checked. A non-null treatment field does not by itself establish that an assessment exists, that a date is known, or that an event falls inside an indicator window.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Match rows where the resolved field is null.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field IS NULL

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Finding missing values in rows supplied by a measurable.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Field in an available row AbsenceRule selects it? 1100 No 0 No: zero is not SQL NULL NULL Yes No row supplied by the measurable No row exists for the rule to select

A measurable may deliberately provide one row per cancer with a null field when no linked record exists; in that case the rule can select that row. Without such a row, AbsenceRule cannot find the cancer by looking for nulls. Missing documentation also does not establish clinical absence. For “eligible cancers with no qualifying surgery evidence”, use an eligible-cancer measure EXCEPT a surgery measure, with the appropriate episode and timing definitions.

Existing definitions can also combine a dated positive criterion with an AbsenceRule through AND. For example, stage recorded on 10 January AND a supplied no-surgery row qualifies on 10 January. The absence condition has no event date and does not erase the stage date. A required event with a missing date still cannot establish a completion date. Absence alone cannot establish that something happened inside a date window.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
Apply a threshold comparison to a measurable's numeric value column.

Supported threshold directions:

  • >
  • <
  • =
  • !=

Scalar rules also carry a threshold_comparator target, which tells the engine which measurable exposes the numeric column to compare against.

docs.title: Concept filtering behavior
docs.text:
Scalar rules have two modes:

  • concept_id = 0: threshold-only comparison, no concept restriction
  • concept_id != 0: threshold comparison constrained to a concept-like field

This is an important current usage detail:

  • numeric-only measurables are valid for threshold-only scalar rules
  • concept-constrained scalar rules require the target measurable to expose both value_numeric_attr and value_concept_attr

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text:
Threshold-only scalar rule:

numeric_value_column < threshold

Concept-constrained scalar rule:

field = concept_id
AND numeric_value_column < threshold

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text:
• treatment within 30 days of death
  • diagnosis to treatment interval
  • referral-to-specialist interval
  • measurement thresholds such as ECOG, lab values, or scores

docs.title: Worked example: a time threshold
docs.text:
Suppose the measurable exposes an interval in whole days. With concept_id=0, scalar_threshold=30 and threshold_direction=lt, the rule tests only whether that interval is less than 30. Set threshold_comparator to the measurable that supplies the interval.

Interval supplied by the measurable Selected by < 30? −1 day Yes: the rule has no lower bound 29 days Yes 30 days No: < is strict 31 days No NULL No

“Less than 30” is different from “0 through 30 days, inclusive”. For a bounded event-to-event interval, a temporal-window measure makes both bounds and the compared dates explicit.

docs.title: Worked example: a numeric measurement
docs.text:
Suppose concept 3000 identifies a measurement whose numeric score must be less than 2. A concept-constrained scalar rule checks both the measurement concept and its value on the same row.

Measurement concept Numeric value Selected by concept 3000 AND value < 2? 3000 1 Yes 3000 2 No 4000 1 No: wrong measurement 3000 NULL No

With concept_id=0, the 4000 row would also pass the numeric threshold if the measurable supplies it. Use that mode when the measurable already identifies the required quantity, rather than to mix unrelated measurements.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
Match rows using a boolean predicate column exposed by the measurable.

Predicate rules use concept_id as a lightweight boolean flag rather than as an OMOP concept lookup:

  • concept_id is None: predicate must be TRUE
  • concept_id = 1: predicate must be TRUE
  • concept_id = 0: predicate must be FALSE
  • any other non-zero value is coerced to TRUE

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text:
predicate_field IS TRUE

or

predicate_field IS FALSE

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text:
Derived boolean modifiers such as:

  • treatment includes radiotherapy
  • treatment includes systemic therapy
  • concurrent chemo-radiotherapy flag

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Suppose the measurable supplies a derived “includes RT” flag. With concept_id=1 (or omitted), the rule selects true flags. With concept_id=0, it selects false flags.

Flag supplied by the measurable Select true (concept_id=1) Select false (concept_id=0) TRUE Yes No FALSE No Yes NULL No No

An unknown flag is not a false flag. The predicate’s clinical meaning comes from the measurable that calculates it; the rule only tests that result.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Expand a phenotype definition into a curated set of concepts and match any of them.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field IN (phenotype_concept_ids)

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Curated research or histology-driven definitions that do not map cleanly onto a single hierarchy.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Suppose phenotype 7 explicitly contains concepts 1100 and 2000. A PhenotypeRule with phenotype_id=7 tests membership in that set.

Recorded concept Selected? 1100 Yes 2000 Yes 1200 No: not in the curated set NULL No

Being related to a member is not enough. Include the desired descendants in the phenotype definition if the clinical question requires them.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
Match rows whose resolved string field contains the source concept's concept_code.

In practice this is usually used against measurable string fields that store code- or label-like values.

docs.title: SQL shape
docs.text: field ILIKE '%concept_code%'

docs.title: Typical use
docs.text: Matching code or label fragments where a suitable coded definition is unavailable.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Suppose the rule’s referenced concept has concept_code='ABC'. The rule uses that code as its search fragment against the measurable’s string field.

String supplied by the measurable Selected? Why ABC.1 Yes Contains ABC abc.2 Yes Matching is case-insensitive XABCY Yes The fragment can occur anywhere ABD.1 No Does not contain ABC NULL No No string to match

This is a contains test, not a prefix or vocabulary-hierarchy test. It does not validate the coding system. The % and _ characters in a search fragment also act as SQL wildcards; they are not escaped as literal characters.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Rule type Primary measurable field Typical purpose ExactRule concept precise coded match HierarchyRule concept inclusive concept family HierarchyExclusionRule concept exclusion family PresenceRule concept-like field any recorded value AbsenceRule concept-like field null value in an existing row ScalarRule numeric, optionally concept thresholds and time windows PredicateRule predicate derived booleans PhenotypeRule concept curated concept-set expansion SubstringRule string code/label substring match

docs.title: From selected records to an indicator result
docs.text:
Rules keep the dates and cancer identities supplied by their measurable. They do not reassign evidence across primaries or reduce it to one patient result.

Selected evidence for one patient What it establishes Two qualifying assessments for cancer A, on different dates Both can remain available for later date-window checks A qualifying assessment for cancer B Evidence for B; it cannot satisfy A’s indicator through same-cancer matching A record with a qualifying code but no date Code matching can succeed; dated eligibility or a timing window still needs the required date

Episode attachment explains where evidence belongs. Evidence and indicators explains how dates, eligibility and counting cancers or patients determine the final result.

docs.title: Schema Management
docs.text: The dashboard database holds the tables that describe reports, indicators, measures, subqueries, and rules. Those tables are versioned with Alembic, and oa-cohorts schema is the interface to them.

docs.title: Rebuilding and refreshing clinical materialized views
docs.text:
Clinical materialized views are defined by omop-constructs in the CDM database. The dashboard-table migrations described below manage report configuration tables; oa-cohorts schema upgrade does not replace those clinical view definitions.

If source data changes while the view definition stays the same, refresh the affected views in dependency order and update their statistics. For an individual view, the operator commands are:

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW schema_name.view_name;
ANALYZE schema_name.view_name;

Replace the example schema and view names with the verified target. Installing a new package does not change definitions already stored in PostgreSQL, and a refresh uses the stored definition.

If a definition changes, rebuild the affected views and their dependent objects during an approved maintenance window. Preserve their definitions, ownership, grants and custom indexes for restoration or rollback; drop dependents before the views they reference, then recreate in dependency order. ANALYZE each populated view immediately after creating it, before building its dependents. Check the release's rebuild scope and verify the report results before reopening report jobs.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The current schema is the baseline. To bring a database under management:

oa-cohorts schema bootstrap

On an existing database this checks that the schema matches the models and then records it as revision 0001_baseline without running any DDL. If it does not match, bootstrap stops and reports what differs — stamping a mismatched schema as the baseline would make that mismatch permanent and invisible. Pass --adopt-on-drift if the difference is known and intentional.

On an empty database the same command creates the tables and records the revision.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
• schema check compares the live schema to the models and lists every difference. Exits non-zero when they disagree, so oa-cohorts schema check --quiet works as a deployment gate.
  • schema status shows the current revision, the head, and anything pending between them.
  • schema bootstrap creates or adopts, as above.
  • schema upgrade applies pending migrations.
  • schema sql prints the SQL an upgrade would run without executing it, for review or for handing to whoever owns the database.
  • schema history lists the revisions.

docs.title: Drift warnings during normal work
docs.text:
Every command that opens the dashboard database checks the schema first, so a mismatch surfaces when you were about to use the data rather than after something has already failed.

Read commands — report-summary, indicator-summary, measure-summary — print a warning and carry on, since their results are still worth seeing with the caveat attached. import-config stops instead, because a config import that fails partway through a mismatched schema leaves a partly loaded database that re-running will not fix. Use --ignore-schema-drift to import anyway.

If a command fails with a database error regardless, the error is re-checked against the live schema and any mismatch reported as the likely cause, so a bare no such column: report.report_owner arrives with an explanation.

docs.title: What an import does to a column your CSV does not have
docs.text:
import-config upserts on primary key: a row whose non-key columns differ from the stored row is updated. Two rules govern the columns a file omits, and they matter most for report_indicator_map, whose override values are authored by hand and cannot be regenerated from anything.

  • A column absent from the CSV is left alone. The file has no opinion about it, so the stored value stands and the row does not count as replaced.
  • A column present but empty is set to NULL. That is an instruction, and it is how a value is deliberately cleared through the transport.

The distinction is the difference between "this export predates the column" and "this export wants the column cleared", which a plain empty-vs-missing comparison cannot tell apart. Before it existed, a narrow CSV imported against a database holding overrides emitted UPDATE report_indicator_map SET WHERE ... — a bare SQL syntax error rather than either outcome.

docs.title: Enum values are not checked
docs.text:
schema check uses Alembic's comparison, which inspects column types but never the set of values an existing enum accepts. Adding a member to RuleTemporality, or to any other rule enum, produces no revision and no warning — it fails when a row using the new value is written.

Enum changes therefore need their ALTER TYPE added to the migration by hand. sync_enum_labels does that idempotently:

from oa_cohorts.schema.enum_ops import sync_enum_labels

def upgrade() -> None:
    sync_enum_labels("ruletemporality", (
        "dt_any", "dt_current_start", ..., "dt_referral",
    ))

It emits ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS for each label, so it adds only what is missing and is safe to re-run. It also does nothing on SQLite, where these columns are plain VARCHAR. Pass the full label set rather than just the new one, so the revision stays reproducible.

Because it is idempotent it can sit in a revision that also creates the type — 0001_baseline does exactly that, as the pattern to copy. Note that ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE cannot run inside a transaction on Postgres older than 12; the helper raises a clear error rather than failing obscurely.

docs.title: Adding a migration
docs.text:
Model changes need a revision. Generate one against a scratch database rather than production:

import sqlalchemy as sa
from oa_cohorts.schema import revise, upgrade

engine = sa.create_engine("sqlite:///scratch.db")
upgrade(engine)                                  # bring it to the current head
revise(engine, "add referral temporality")
Do not edit 0001_baseline.py to track model changes. It is a frozen snapshot of the schema at the point migrations were introduced, and schema check reporting clean depends on it staying in step with the models it describes. Notes:

  • Keep the revision id inside 32 characters. alembic_version.version_num is VARCHAR(32). A longer id applies its DDL and then fails writing the version row — and only on Postgres, since SQLite does not enforce varchar length. The result is a database whose schema has changed but whose recorded revision has not. test_revision_ids_fit_the_alembic_version_column guards this.
  • copy_from needs the table as it is before the direction being run. A revision that adds columns and drops them again needs two frozen shapes, not one: batch mode drops columns from the description it was given, so handing downgrade the pre-add shape fails with KeyError on the first column it cannot find.

docs.title: Adopting a database older than the models
docs.text:
schema bootstrap stamps head, which asserts the live schema matches the current models. When it does not, the database is not necessarily broken — it may simply match an earlier revision, with the difference being migrations that have never been applied.

oa-cohorts schema bootstrap --revision 0001_baseline
oa-cohorts schema upgrade

bootstrap refuses to stamp head in that situation rather than claiming migrations ran that never did — which would leave 0002 permanently unapplied and the column types permanently wrong.

--adopt-on-drift is the different case — a difference that is known and intentional and that no migration will resolve. It repairs nothing and should not be used to get past an unapplied migration.

docs.title: Evidence and indicator policies
docs.text:
Migration 0006_resolution_policy adds settings for matching evidence, selecting treatments, choosing reference dates and reporting periods, and accepting undated records. See the configuration reference and worked examples for what each setting means.

Existing definitions keep their IDs and whether they count cancers or patients. The migration does not choose new clinical intervals; indicator windows still use the cohort date unless configured otherwise.

Test an upgrade on a copy of the configuration database before applying it to a live report. Read-only report execution does not run migrations automatically. Downgrading refuses to discard nondefault policy values, so review and reset those settings deliberately before reverting. This migration changes only oa-cohorts configuration tables; it does not rebuild clinical materialized views.
